new.title: Climb the tower of the Grote Kerk in Breda
new.desc: The Brabantine Gothic Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekerk rises almost 100 metres above the Grote Markt. Inside, the Prinsenkapel holds the tombs of the Nassau family, ancestors of the Dutch royal house.
new.tip: The church itself is free to walk into; the tower climb needs a ticket and goes up a few hundred steps, so pick a clear day for views as far as Antwerp's skyline.

new.title: Find the Spanjaardsgat by Breda Castle
new.desc: This 17th century water gate between two round towers guarded the castle moat. Locals tie it to the 1590 peat boat ruse, when soldiers hidden under turf on a barge took the castle back from the Spanish, even though the gate itself was built later.
new.tip: The castle houses the Royal Military Academy, so you can only look from outside; the best view of gate and castle is from the quay by the Haven and from Valkenberg park.

new.title: Admire the wavy roof of the Chassé Theater
new.desc: Herman Hertzberger designed Breda's theatre in the 1990s with a rolling roof that hides its two stage towers, inspired by a Giacometti sculpture of a sleeping woman.
new.tip: Walk around the building from the Claudius Prinsenlaan side to see the roof waves best, then catch a show or film inside.

new.title: Meet the Nassaus at Stedelijk Museum Breda
new.desc: The city museum on the Boschstraat mixes Breda's history, art and design, with a permanent exhibition on the Nassau family who made the town their seat.
new.tip: Combine it with a beer at De Beyerd, a few doors down the same street.

new.title: Stroll the gardens of Kasteel Bouvigne
new.desc: On the edge of the Mastbos stands a moated castle with a tower and stepped gables, once owned by the Oranges. Its formal gardens are open to everyone.
new.tip: The gardens are open on weekdays only and the interior just a few days a year, so plan a weekday visit and continue into the Mastbos.

new.title: Grab a terrace seat on the Havermarkt
new.desc: Tucked behind the Grote Kerk, the Havermarkt is a small square packed with café terraces, the place where Breda comes to drink in the sun. Breda is known for some of the best terraces in the south.
new.tip: Look for the bronze troubadour statue on the square before you sit down.

new.title: Drink a house brew at Café De Beyerd
new.desc: This brewery café on the Boschstraat brews its own beers and pours them with Dutch bar snacks; it is also the starting point of Breda's guided beer walks.
new.tip: Order a tasting tray of their own beers and a plate of bitterballen.
new.q: Café Brouwerij De Beyerd Boschstraat 26 Breda

new.title: Have a beer among 1,000 signs at the Bierreclame Museum
new.desc: In Princenhage, west of the centre, a bar is plastered with about a thousand old enamel beer signs and posters. It is a museum you visit with a glass in hand.
new.tip: It opens on Sundays only, so make it the end of a Sunday bike ride to the Mastbos.

new.title: Sip a drink on the sand at Belcrum Beach
new.desc: North of the station, in the old harbour and auction district of Belcrum, an urban beach with deckchairs sits right on the water of the Mark.
new.tip: Arrive early on sunny days or go on a weekday; the walk there takes you through the creative Belcrum neighbourhood.

new.title: Join carnival when Breda becomes Kielegat
new.desc: For four days before Lent, Breda renames itself Kielegat and parties in costume. Highlights are the big parade on Monday and the burning of the dolls Kiske and Mieske on the Grote Markt on Tuesday evening.
new.tip: Events start at 11 minutes past the hour (the fool's number). Dress up: nobody goes out in plain clothes.

new.title: Walk the 500-year-old Mastbos
new.desc: Planted from 1515 by the Nassaus, the Mastbos is one of the oldest planted forests in the Netherlands. Its timber went into Breda Castle and later into ship masts, and Prince Maurits laid straight hunting lanes through it that still aim at distant church towers.
new.tip: Follow the Eeuwigheidslaantje, a lane that runs dead straight through the whole forest, and end at Kasteel Bouvigne on its northern edge.

new.title: Watch weavers at work in the TextielMuseum
new.desc: Tilburg's textile museum fills the former Mommers wool mill. Besides old looms you can look into the TextielLab, where designers and artists produce new work on modern machines.
new.tip: Head for the windows of the TextielLab on a weekday, when the machines are most likely to be running.

new.title: Find Tilburg's oldest chapel at the Hasseltplein
new.desc: The little brick Hasseltse kapel dates from around 1536, making it the oldest religious building in Tilburg. It was once even used as a house before Mary returned; her 18th century wooden bust still has a wardrobe of robes and pilgrims' jewellery.
new.tip: Look at the bronze Mary statue in the triangular park next to it; the chapel is busiest in May, the month of Mary.

new.title: Meet Brabant's wildlife at the Natuurmuseum
new.desc: Right opposite Tilburg station, the Natuurmuseum Brabant shows the animals, plants and landscapes of the province in changing exhibitions.
new.tip: Handy when you have time before a train; it has its own museum café.

new.title: See the palace King Willem II never lived in
new.desc: Willem II loved Tilburg so much that he ordered a palace there, but he died just before it was finished in 1849. Today the Paleis-Raadhuis is the city's wedding hall, and the young Vincent van Gogh went to school in it.
new.tip: Look at the little corner towers from the Stadhuisplein, then find the statue of Willem II on the Heuvel.

new.title: Taste Schrobbelèr, Tilburg's carnival liqueur
new.desc: This sweet herbal liqueur was dreamed up in 1973 by a Tilburg man with a weak stomach and is still distilled in the city. It comes in a stone jug and is drunk chilled, above all at carnival.
new.tip: Ask for one in Café Tribunaal, the big brown café on the Korte Heuvel.

new.title: Try the taps at LOC Brewery in the Spoorzone
new.desc: Born as a hobby in 2014, Tilburg's own craft brewery now runs a brew pub in the old railway yards with around twenty rotating taps.
new.tip: Come for lunch or a borrel after a visit to the LocHal across the square.

new.title: Dine in a country house at Hofstede de Blaak
new.desc: Near the Oude Warande forest, this restaurant fills a historic English-style manor house, with a garden terrace in summer.
new.tip: Book ahead and pair dinner with a walk along the star lanes of the Oude Warande.

new.title: Ride the Tilburgse Kermis on Roze Maandag
new.desc: Every July the biggest funfair in the Benelux fills Tilburg's centre for ten days. Its Monday is Roze Maandag, a pink, glittery day of acceptance with a Pride Walk, drag shows and parties.
new.tip: Join the free Pride Walk from the station around midday, or arrive on the party train from Rotterdam.

new.title: See a gig at 013
new.desc: Named after Tilburg's old phone code, 013 is one of the largest pop venues in the Netherlands and home to Roadburn, a cult festival for heavy and experimental music.
new.tip: Check the small hall too: it books up and coming bands for much less money.

new.title: Find the centre of the Oude Warande star forest
new.desc: Laid out in 1712, the Oude Warande is one of the few intact star forests in the Netherlands: eight straight lanes radiate from a single point in the middle of a square of woods.
new.tip: Stand at the central crossing and look down each lane in turn; the forest is right next to Tilburg Universiteit station.

new.title: Crawl through the Doloris art maze
new.desc: In Tilburg's Spoorzone, the Meta Maze is a surreal labyrinth of more than 40 rooms full of strange objects and hidden passages that you explore by climbing and crawling.
new.tip: Wear clothes you can crawl in and book a slot online; it is not suitable for young children.

new.title: Walk the ramparts of Willemstad's star fort
new.desc: William of Orange fortified Willemstad in 1583, and its seven-pointed star of bastions and moats is still almost complete. Inside you find the domed Koepelkerk and the Gouvernementshuis built for Prince Maurits.
new.tip: Walk the full loop on top of the walls, passing the d'Orangemolen windmill by the harbour.

new.title: Admire the town hall of Klundert
new.desc: The small fortress town of Klundert has a richly decorated town hall from 1621, built on the orders of Prince Maurits, standing in the middle of the old ramparts.
new.tip: Combine it with Willemstad, a few kilometres west; both towns guarded the Hollands Diep.

new.title: Visit Van Gogh's birthplace in Zundert
new.desc: Vincent van Gogh was born in 1853 in the parsonage on Zundert's market square. The Vincent van GoghHuis on that spot tells the story of his Brabant childhood and his bond with his brother Theo.
new.tip: Use the audio tour in which Vincent himself talks, then walk the Van Gogh route through the village.

new.title: Watch the dahlia floats of the Corso Zundert
new.desc: On the first Sunday of September, twenty Zundert hamlets parade giant floats covered entirely in dahlias, millions of them, most grown in the village itself. The tradition is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
new.tip: Come on the Monday after, when the floats are on display and the crowds are smaller.

new.title: See where Vincent became an artist in Etten-Leur
new.desc: Vincent's father preached in this small church on the Markt in Etten, and in 1881 Vincent set up his first studio in the parsonage behind it and registered as an artist. Stained glass, films and panels now tell that story.
new.tip: Book tickets online, then cross the Markt to the Oude Raadhuis where he signed the register.

new.title: Spot the little castles of Oosterhout
new.desc: Oosterhout has a unique cluster of slotjes, moated farmhouses that grew into small noble residences from the 15th century. Five of them line the Ridderstraat next to the Slotpark.
new.tip: They are private homes, so admire them from the street; a walking loop continues to the slotje De Blauwe Camer and the abbeys outside town.

new.title: Learn how leather was made at De Looierij in Dongen
new.desc: Around 1890 Dongen had more tanneries than anywhere else in the Netherlands. Museum De Looierij, in an old tannery on the Kerkstraat, shows the whole tanning process.
new.tip: Walk the Hoge Ham afterwards to see the old leather factories and the tanners' villas.

new.title: Taste a village brew at De Roos in Hilvarenbeek
new.desc: The village brewery of Hilvarenbeek, dating from 1877, is now a volunteer-run museum where you see how beer was brewed over a wood fire. The tasting room pours house beers like the Bikse Tripel.
new.tip: It is open on weekend afternoons; cycle there from Tilburg in under an hour through the countryside.
new.q: Museumbrouwerij De Roos Sint Sebastiaanstraat 4 Hilvarenbeek

new.title: Have a drink at the oldest hotel in the Netherlands
new.desc: Hotel De Draak on the Grote Markt of Bergen op Zoom already stood before the city fire of 1397, which makes it the oldest hotel in the country; its cellars date from the 14th century.
new.tip: Sit on the terrace facing the market and the Peperbus church tower, then walk to the Gevangenpoort.
new.q: Grand Hotel De Draak Grote Markt Bergen op Zoom

new.title: Find Bronze Age burial mounds on the Regte Heide
new.desc: South of Goirle, the hilly Regte Heide is a stretch of heath with seven Bronze Age burial mounds, some ringed again with wooden posts, above the stream valley of the Oude Leij.
new.tip: Go in August when the heather is purple; from Tilburg it is an easy bike ride via Goirle.
